top_choice_rationale: P001 (B005: Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn) does best on the common test. The random-coefficients demand framework with endogenous prices changed what can be credibly estimated about substitution, market power and merger effects. It has about three decades of use and scrutiny in merger review, antitrust, regulation and applied work. Once the citation is limited to demand and competition in differentiated-product markets, the three names match one jointly authored core, which resolves my opening attribution objection. The main reservations are that it is a methods prize, that estimates are sensitive to implementation, and that the three-name cap leaves out Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin. The citation should therefore state that it rewards a method. I rank P002 (B030: Autor, Hanson, Dorn) second because its design-based evidence on labour-market adjustment is substantive and the trio is attributable. Its maturity is lower, since persistence, magnitude and shift-share identification are still debated. P000 is last because the slate contains a mature, well-attributed candidate. B027, which I preferred in round 1, is not on the slate. I did not move because ten members support P001, since support counts are not evidence of merit. I have not independently verified the claims about use, replication or prior prizes in the round-2 statements.
recusal_note: No tie to Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn, Autor, Hanson or Dorn is apparent from my profile. My profile lists Per Krusell (secretary) and John Hassler (chair) as co-authors and IIES colleagues. Both now explicitly support P001, so agreement with them is not independent confirmation. My long-running co-author Peter Klenow is on B046, which is not on the slate. This is disclosed but not adjudicated.
